title: Ascites and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in cirrhosis (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Ascites in adults with cirrhosis in India: diagnostic paracentesis, salt restriction, diuretics, large-volume paracentesis with albumin, refractory ascites, and diagnosis, treatment and prophylaxis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), using the BSG/BASL ascites guideline (2020), the ICMR Acute Liver Failure / ACLF STW (2020) and NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025.
findings: Diagnostic paracentesis indications, SAAG 11 g/L or more for portal hypertension, SBP as ascitic neutrophils above 250/mm³, albumin 1.5 g/kg then 1 g/kg on day 3, salt 5–6.5 g/day, spironolactone 100–400 mg, furosemide 40–160 mg, weight-loss limits, albumin 8 g per litre for paracentesis over 5 L, secondary SBP prophylaxis doses and TIPSS cautions checked against BSG/BASL 2020.

SBP regimens (piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly for 7–10 days; cefoperazone-sulbactam alternative) checked against NTG 2025 section 4.7; ceftriaxone 1 g twice daily, albumin and terlipressin against the ICMR ACLF STW.
unverifiedSections: BSG/BASL notes cefotaxime is the most studied antibiotic but recommends local protocols; Indian sources differ (NTG: piperacillin-tazobactam; ICMR: ceftriaxone). Both are shown.
Norfloxacin availability varies in India; ciprofloxacin or co-trimoxazole are alternatives.
Avoidance of NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors is standard practice, not confirmed in the opened extract.
Paediatric ascites is outside the scope of the cited sources.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Ascites is the commonest complication of cirrhosis and marks decompensation. Portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilatation reduce effective arterial volume, activating renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic systems, so the kidneys retain sodium and water that leak into the peritoneum. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source, often with few symptoms, and can trigger kidney failure and encephalopathy. Every patient admitted with ascites needs a diagnostic tap; an ascitic neutrophil count above 250/mm³ means SBP (BSG/BASL 2020). Treatment combines moderate salt restriction, diuretics, paracentesis with albumin and early antibiotics for infection.
keyMechanisms: Portal hypertension raises sinusoidal pressure and lymph formation.
Splanchnic vasodilatation lowers effective arterial volume and activates sodium retention.
Gut bacteria translocate to ascitic fluid with low protein and poor opsonic activity, causing SBP.
Infection and large fluid shifts can precipitate hepatorenal syndrome.

symptoms: Fever, abdominal pain, confusion or diarrhoea in SBP
redFlags: Fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy or worsening kidney function: tap for SBP at once (BSG/BASL)
Gastrointestinal bleeding with ascites: needs antibiotic prophylaxis (BSG/BASL recommendation 2.7)
Sodium below 125 mmol/L or rising creatinine on diuretics
precipitants: Alcohol, hepatitis B or C, MASLD
Dietary salt excess, non-adherence to diuretics

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: SAAG below 11 g/L, malignant cells on cytology.
SAAG below 11 g/L, lymphocytic fluid, high ADA; common in India.
Raised JVP, SAAG 11 g/L or more with high protein.
Very high neutrophils, multiple organisms, perforation on imaging; needs surgery.

clinicalManagement.title: Diagnostic paracentesis
actions: Tap every new ascites and every cirrhotic admission with ascites without delay (BSG/BASL recommendations 1.1, 2.1).
Routine INR or platelet checks before paracentesis are not needed (BSG/BASL recommendation 5.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat SBP
actions: Start IV antibiotics (see medicines) and albumin 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours, then 1 g/kg on day 3 if creatinine is raised or rising (BSG/BASL recommendation 6.3).
Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins in acute kidney injury (AKI) (ICMR STW).
Suspected hepatorenal syndrome: terlipressin with albumin (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Uncomplicated ascites
actions: Salt 5–6.5 g/day; no added salt; avoid precooked meals (BSG/BASL recommendations 3.1–3.2).
Spironolactone; add furosemide for recurrent or tense ascites (BSG/BASL recommendations 4.1–4.2).
Weight loss no more than 0.5 kg/day without oedema, 1 kg/day with oedema (BSG/BASL).
Stop diuretics in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia; fluid restriction 1–1.5 L/day only if hypervolaemic with sodium below 125 mmol/L (BSG/BASL recommendations 4.3–4.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Tense or refractory ascites
actions: Large-volume paracentesis with albumin 8 g per litre removed when over 5 L (BSG/BASL recommendation 6.1).
Refractory: consider TIPSS with caution, or transplant referral; palliative care if not a transplant candidate (BSG/BASL recommendations 7.1, 12.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Prevent SBP
actions: Antibiotic prophylaxis for gastrointestinal bleeding with ascites (BSG/BASL recommendation 2.7).

medicationPlan.note: Diuretic, albumin and prophylaxis doses from BSG/BASL 2020; SBP antibiotic regimens from NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 and the ICMR ACLF STW. India-only topic; the Saudi topic is unchanged. Not clinically reviewed.

teaching.scope: Cirrhotic ascites and SBP in India.
learningObjectives: Tap every admitted patient with ascites.
Diagnose and treat SBP with antibiotics and albumin.
keyPoints: Albumin 1.5 g/kg then 1 g/kg on day 3.
Albumin 8 g per litre for paracentesis over 5 L.
pitfalls: Not tapping because the patient looks well.
Continuing diuretics in AKI or sodium below 125.
